analysis.one_liner: Requires credit bureaus to show consumers their own credit scores and risk scores on request.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote: after a September 2000 hearing it sat in a House subcommittee and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: At the time, credit bureaus and scoring companies computed credit scores that lenders used to decide who gets loans and at what rates, but the law did not require them to show those scores to the people being scored. This bill would have amended the Fair Credit Reporting Act so a consumer could get everything in their file, including credit scores and any other risk scores. It was introduced by Rep. Chris Cannon with bipartisan cosponsors, got a subcommittee hearing in September 2000, and was never brought to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers applying for mortgages, car loans, credit cards, or insurance. Today a three-digit score decides whether you get credit and what you pay for it, but under the law as written consumers had no right to see that number. The bill would have let anyone request the complete contents of their file, including the score lenders see, so they could check it for errors, understand why they were turned down, and fix problems before applying. It also would have ended the practice of charging consumers for information already collected about them.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Fair Credit Reporting Act so a consumer reporting agency must, on request, disclose all information in the consumer's file, including credit scores and any other risk scores or predictors relating to the consumer.
Current law required file disclosure but explicitly did not require disclosure of credit or risk scores, leaving consumers unable to see the number their lenders used.
The bill was introduced with bipartisan support: 8 cosponsors split evenly between 4 Republicans and 4 Democrats.

analysis.who_pays: The three national credit reporting bureaus (Experian, Equifax, TransUnion) and the scoring companies whose formulas produce the scores. They would have to hand over score information on request, develop systems to do so, and give up the ability to keep scores secret or sell them to lenders while withholding them from consumers.

drawbacks.text: Disclosure imposes compliance costs on consumer reporting agencies, which would need to build systems to package and deliver score data to consumers on request.

A bare score without context can mislead: the bill requires disclosure of scores and predictors but does not require the explanation, scale, or factor detail a consumer would need to act on the number, and lenders' underwriting formulas could still weigh undisclosed predictors.
The bill is a one-line amendment; it does not address the accuracy of the underlying data in consumer files, which consumer advocates identified as the deeper problem with credit reporting.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to ordinary people is real and large relative to the cost: a few lines of statutory language forcing disclosure of information the bureaus already maintain, versus consumers finally being able to see the scores that gate access to credit. The main weakness is design, not cost; disclosing a number without a plain-language explanation limits how useful it is, and it leaves data accuracy problems untouched. Even so, the change is far more costly to the bureaus' business model than to anyone else.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Banking and Financial Services Committee, then to its consumer credit subcommittee, which held a hearing in September 2000, but the bill was never marked up or brought to the floor and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Cannon introduced the Fair Credit Full Disclosure Act on September 14, 1999.
The House referred it to the Committee on Banking and Financial Services the day it was introduced, where it sat without a markup.
On September 24, 1999, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit.
The subcommittee held a hearing on September 21, 2000, but no further action followed.
The bill never received a vote in the full House, and the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit bureaus and scoring companies, which kept scores out of consumers' hands and continued selling data and score access to lenders. Consumers remained unable to see the numbers used to judge them until later legislation and industry changes forced disclosure.

against.name: Consumer credit reporting and scoring industry

against.what_they_did: Fought credit score disclosure generally, keeping scores available to lenders but not to consumers; this industry opposition is a well-known backdrop to score-disclosure bills of that era, though it is not documented in the bill's record.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was evenly split, 4 Republican and 4 Democratic cosponsors behind a Republican sponsor; the record shows no party-line fight, only inaction.

industries.industry: Consumer credit reporting bureaus (Experian, Equifax, TransUnion)
industries.note: Their business is compiling consumer data and selling it and score access to lenders; the bill would have forced them to give consumers the scores on request, a direct cost to a model built on consumers not seeing their own numbers.

Score formulas were proprietary and sold to lenders; mandatory disclosure to consumers would have ended the arrangement where the scored party could not see the score. This is how the score gatekeeping was entrenched before disclosure became standard.
They rely on the same scores; disclosure lets applicants anticipate decisions and fix errors, which cuts down on surprises for lenders but imposes no direct obligation on them.
